who: a lone wolf still crouched over a fresh kill
place: a frost-stiff meadow at dawn, half a mile from the treeline, where sound carries far
present: a fresh deer carcass, mostly eaten
a stranger on foot, walking closer without seeing the wolf yet
a pair of ravens waiting nearby

factors.fact: The wolf has not eaten in three days and this carcass is most of what is left of it.
The approaching figure is upright, on two legs, far larger than the wolf alone.
The wolf's hind leg is stiff from an old injury and running is painful.
The stranger has not yet noticed the wolf or the kill.
The treeline is close enough to reach before the stranger could catch up.
Wolves in this range have learned that upright figures rarely chase far.

could_also.verb: growls a warning and stands over
grabs a mouthful and slinks off
flees for the treeline

would_not.why: the meal isn't worth a fight it can't win on a bad leg
an approaching upright figure this close can't be ignored

then: It waits until the stranger is within thirty paces, then bolts for the trees, leaving most of the kill behind for the ravens.
why: Hunger argues for holding the kill, but the stiff leg means it cannot win a fight or an outright chase if seen too close; leaving early while the gap is still wide costs less than waiting for the choice to be forced.
turns_on: whether the stranger keeps closing the distance

who: a farm's guard dog, chained near the yard gate
place: a farmyard at night, a latecomer at the gate, the family asleep in the house
present: a wooden gate with a metal latch
a stranger standing just outside it
a lit window in the farmhouse, distant
the dog's chain, staked to a post

factors.fact: The yard inside the gate is the dog's whole world; it has never once let a stranger cross the fence.
The stranger has just rattled the latch, testing whether it's locked.
The chain lets the dog reach the gate itself but no farther.
The dog knows the household's voices and has never heard this one before.
It is well past midnight, when the household is used to full silence, not barking.
Nothing in the yard has ever hurt the dog badly enough to make it wary of a fight.

does.verb: lunges to the end of its chain, barking

could_also.verb: stands stiff-legged and growls low
barks toward

would_not.why: a stranger touching the latch at night is exactly what it exists to announce

would_not.verb: slips its chain and gives chase
would_not.why: the chain holds and it has never tested it hard enough to know otherwise

then: The barking wakes a light in the farmhouse; the stranger lets go of the latch and backs off into the dark before anyone comes out.
why: The rattled latch is exactly the kind of act the dog exists to punish, and raising the house costs it nothing while its own reach ends at the chain; noise, not a bite it cannot deliver, is the only option within its power.
turns_on: whether the stranger reaches for the latch

who: a middle-aged tenant farmer, quick to take offense
place: a village tavern on market night, crowded enough that words carry
present: a second farmer who owes him for a torn fence
a room full of other patrons
a barkeep wiping down the counter

factors.fact: The other farmer just called him a thief in front of the room, over a debt that isn't settled.
Half the tavern turned to listen when the words landed.
He is in fact owed money for the fence, so the insult stings worse for being aimed the wrong way.
In this village, an insult left unanswered in public is remembered for years.
The other farmer is younger and has hit men before over less.
He can demand the debt be settled aloud, which shifts the room's judgment without a blow.

could_also.verb: shoves
turns and walks out
insults back

would_not.why: he'd lose that fight and knows it

would_not.verb: laughs it off and buys a round
would_not.why: letting it pass in front of this room costs him standing he can't spare

then: The room's murmurs turn against the younger farmer once the debt is named; he mutters an apology and pays a portion before the night is out.
why: Public standing and the unpaid debt both point toward answering in words the room will judge, since a swing he'd lose settles nothing and silence would be remembered longer than the insult itself.
turns_on: whether other men in the tavern are watching

who: a cart-driver hauling goods to market
place: a narrow forest road at dusk, no one else in sight for a mile either way
present: a stranger blocking the road with a drawn knife
a cart loaded with sacks of grain
a mule hitched to the cart

factors.fact: The stranger has a knife out and is asking for the coin purse, not the grain.
The coin is this month's rent, already promised to the landholder.
He is unarmed except for a cart-whip within reach.
Losing the coin means missing rent, but losing his life means missing everything.
Help is a mile off in either direction, too far to matter now.
The stranger has not yet touched him, only shown the blade.

could_also.verb: throws the purse and drives off
tries to bargain, offering grain instead

would_not.why: a whip against a knife at arm's length is a losing trade for a purse of coin
the coin isn't worth what a drawn knife is willing to cost him

then: He hands the purse over and is let go; he arrives home short on rent and has to ask the landholder for a week's grace.
why: The knife already drawn and no help within reach make the choice arithmetic, not pride: the coin can be earned again, the life spent tonight cannot, so it goes over the moment the blade stays out.
turns_on: how sharp the knife looks

who: a mother bear foraging with two cubs at her side
place: a berry slope in late summer, wind blowing from the hiker toward her, cubs feeding a short way off
present: two cubs, feeding on berries a few strides away
a hiker who has just crested the rise
a patch of dense brush between her and the hiker

factors.fact: The cubs are close enough that the hiker's path will pass between her and them.
The hiker is forty paces off and hasn't seen the cubs yet.
An upright human is not something she'd challenge over food alone.
Nothing in her life has taught her that this distance is safe with cubs this small.
She could call the cubs to her and retreat into the brush before being seen at all.

could_also.verb: charges a few steps and stops
gathers the cubs and retreats

would_not.why: a human this far off isn't yet worth the risk of a real fight
the path he's on runs too close to the cubs to ignore

then: The huff and bluff stop the hiker in his tracks; he backs away slowly, and she herds the cubs off into the brush the moment his back is turned enough.
why: The cubs' closeness argues for driving the danger off now, but the human isn't yet close enough to justify a real charge, so a bluff that costs nothing but noise does the job the situation actually calls for.
turns_on: how far the cubs have wandered from her

who: an old farm dog that sleeps by the henhouse
place: a henhouse yard at night, a hole freshly dug under the wire fence
present: a fox, halfway through a gap under the fence, a dead hen already in its jaws
a coop full of remaining hens, panicking
the farmhouse, dark and asleep

factors.fact: The henhouse is the one thing the dog has guarded every night of its life.
The fox has already killed one hen and is halfway out with it.
The dog is old and slower than it once was, but the fox is half in, half out of the gap and slowed by the load in its jaws.
If it catches the fox before it clears the gap, the fox can't run.
One hen is already dead; the rest can still be saved.

could_also.verb: barks to scare it off without catching it
stands guard over the remaining hens instead

would_not.verb: chases it once it's clear of the fence
would_not.why: a fox running free in the open is faster than an old dog now

would_not.verb: ignores it and lets it finish taking the hen
would_not.why: the fence and the flock are the one thing it's never once let go unguarded

then: The fox drops the dead hen and squeezes back through the gap just ahead of the dog's jaws, and the remaining hens settle once the dog stands over the hole the rest of the night.
why: The half-cleared gap is the only moment the fox is catchable at all, so the dog spends what speed it has left right then rather than after, when the fox would already be gone.
turns_on: whether the fox is inside the pen or fleeing

who: a local blacksmith, well known and well liked in the village
place: the same village tavern, later on market night, now thinner of witnesses
present: a traveling stranger who has been drinking heavily and mocking the local accent all evening
a handful of remaining patrons, mostly not paying attention anymore
the tavern door, shut against the cold

factors.fact: The stranger has just mocked him by name-calling in front of the few patrons left.
He himself has had enough drink that his temper is shorter than usual.
Almost no one left is paying attention; there's little standing to be won or lost either way.
He is by far the stronger man and knows it.
Striking a stranger over drunk words in an empty room earns no one's respect, win or lose.

does.verb: ignores and turns back to his drink

could_also.verb: tells him to leave
grabs him by the collar

would_not.why: with no one watching there's nothing to win by it and everything to answer for after

would_not.verb: laughs along and buys him another drink
would_not.why: the insult was real enough that ignoring is the best he'll manage, not befriending

then: The stranger tires of getting no reaction and stumbles out into the night alone a short while later.
why: An empty room strips the insult of the audience that would have made an answer worth the risk, and his own drink-shortened temper is exactly the reason to not trust himself to stop at a shove.
turns_on: how many drinks he's had

who: a raccoon that has been rooting through a shed
place: the inside corner of a toolshed, the door swung nearly shut by the person who found it
present: a person holding a rake, blocking most of the doorway
shelves of tools and jars, nowhere else to climb
a narrow gap still open beside the person's leg

factors.fact: There is one narrow gap left beside the person's leg, not yet blocked.
The rake is being held up, not swung yet.
It is a good climber but the shelves lead nowhere but higher into the corner.
It has never fought anything larger than a dog and lost worse than it won.
The gap beside the leg is closing as the person shifts to block it fully.

could_also.verb: hisses and bares teeth, holding ground
climbs the shelving to get higher

would_not.why: nothing it's fought before was this much bigger and won it anything
the one way out is closing and waiting loses it

then: It squeezes past the leg before the gap shuts and is gone into the dark yard before the person can turn around.
why: With an exit still open even by inches, running through it costs far less than a fight against something many times its size, and every moment spent deciding closes the gap further.
turns_on: whether the gap behind it is still open

who: the henyard's longtime rooster
place: a chicken yard at first light, a second, younger rooster newly added to the flock the day before
present: a young rooster brought in yesterday from another farm
the hens, feeding, indifferent for now
a low fence separating this yard from the road

factors.fact: He has held this yard uncontested for two years and every hen in it.
The new rooster crowed first this morning, before he did.
He is heavier and has never lost a yard fight.
The hens have not yet shown any preference between the two.
In this yard, whichever rooster crows first each morning has, in practice, always been the one left standing by evening.

could_also.verb: crows louder over him
struts a wide circle around him first

would_not.verb: backs away and cedes the yard
would_not.why: he has never once lost this yard and nothing about this morning suggests he's weaker now
the challenge came from the other rooster, not from any hen

then: The two roosters spur and flap for a short, loud minute until the younger one breaks and runs for the fence; the yard is his again by full light.
why: Being crowed over first is, by this yard's own history, the opening move of a challenge for the flock, and his unbroken record of winning here means backing down now would cost him standing he has no reason yet to think he's lost.
turns_on: which one crowed first this morning

who: a young shepherd's boy running an errand to town
place: a river ford at midday, the water loud enough to cover raised voices
present: two strangers waiting at the ford, blocking the crossing
a small purse of coin
a sealed letter tucked in his shirt, meant for the town reeve

factors.fact: Two strangers are demanding whatever he's carrying, and he is alone against both.
The coin is his, spendable and replaceable.
The letter isn't his and losing it would fail the person who trusted him with it.
He's fast on foot and knows a shallower crossing upstream they don't.
Both strangers are grown men; he's a boy who can't win a fight against either.

could_also.verb: begs to keep the letter
tries to bolt for the upstream crossing

would_not.verb: hands over the letter as well without a fight
would_not.why: the coin is replaceable but failing the errand he was trusted with is not
two grown men against one boy is a fight he loses before it starts

then: He gives up the coin at once, and when they grab for the letter too he twists free and bolts upstream, reaching the shallower crossing and the town road before either man catches him.
why: The coin is worth handing over the instant two men against one boy make resistance pointless, but the letter carries a trust that isn't his to trade away, so the same logic that surrenders the purse is what makes him run rather than surrender the rest.
turns_on: whether the men are watching the letter or the purse

who: an aging stag, still holding a stretch of oak wood
place: the rutting season, an oak wood at dusk, distant roars closing in
present: a younger, larger stag, roaring back, approaching
a small group of hinds, quiet, watching from cover
open ground between the two rivals

factors.fact: He has held these hinds for three seasons running.
He is lighter than last season and one antler is chipped from an old fight.
The younger stag is heavier and roars louder and longer than he can match.
The hinds are still watching him, not yet drifting toward the newcomer.
In this wood, a stag that doesn't answer a roar loses the hinds without even a fight.

could_also.verb: locks antlers and pushes
turns and leads the hinds off

would_not.why: a straight charge against a heavier animal wastes the one advantage a display might still buy him

would_not.verb: ignores the roar and keeps grazing
would_not.why: an unanswered roar loses the hinds before any fight even happens

then: The display goes on longer than either wants; when the younger stag finally closes to lock antlers, the older one gives ground after a short push and lets the hinds go rather than risk the chipped antler snapping.
why: His weakened frame argues for avoiding a real clash he's likely to lose, but the custom that an unanswered roar loses the herd outright means he has to at least display before he can afford to yield; the retreat comes only once the real cost of the antler is on the line.
turns_on: how much weight the older stag has lost this rut

who: a solitary traveler passing through on foot
place: a narrow lane between two stone walls at dusk, the only through-route to the next village
present: three young strangers blocking the lane ahead, arms crossed
a low wall too high to easily climb with a pack on
a side gap in the wall a short way back, barely noticed

factors.fact: Three strangers stand shoulder to shoulder across the lane, clearly meaning to bar the way.
He is alone and unarmed beyond a walking staff.
He remembers passing a gap in the wall a short way back that they haven't blocked.
They haven't demanded anything yet, only stood in his path.
Turning back in full view of them costs him something, but less than a beating would.

could_also.verb: stops and asks what they want
tries to push straight through

would_not.verb: pushes through the three of them
would_not.why: three against one with no weapon is a fight settled before it starts

would_not.verb: stands his ground and waits them out
would_not.why: waiting doesn't change the numbers and only gives them time to decide to close in

then: He doubles back to the gap and skirts around through a field, adding an hour to his walk but reaching the village well after they've lost interest in waiting.
why: Being outnumbered three to one with no demand yet made means there's nothing to defend by staying, and the remembered gap turns a beating into merely a longer walk, which is the cheaper price by far.
turns_on: whether the gap in the wall is still unblocked

who: a household cat, sunning itself on a low wall
place: a village yard in early afternoon, the neighbor's dog off its rope for once
present: a neighbor's dog, loose and trotting over, curious rather than hostile yet
a low wall the cat is sitting on
a gap in the fence nearby, and another route along the wall itself

factors.fact: The wall is the cat's usual sunning spot, claimed for years.
The dog is much bigger and has chased it before, though never quite caught it.
The wall runs to a gap the dog can't fit through, close behind the cat.
On the wall, the cat has height and the dog cannot easily reach it.

does.verb: arches and hisses, holding its spot

could_also.verb: bolts along the wall to the gap
swats when the dog gets close enough

would_not.verb: jumps down to confront it on open ground
would_not.why: height is the only advantage it has and giving it up would hand the dog every other one
a dog that's chased it before closing this fast can't safely be ignored

then: The dog barks and paws at the wall's base for a minute, then loses interest and wanders off once the cat doesn't come down.
why: Height on the wall neutralizes the size gap that makes the dog dangerous on open ground, so holding that ground and hissing costs nothing while jumping down would trade a safe position for a race it might not win.
turns_on: whether the fence gap is behind the cat or in front of it

who: a middle-aged tanner, well settled in his trade
place: the market square, years after a debt dispute that once cost him his father's land
present: the man who years ago swindled him out of his father's land, now old and using a cane
a crowd of market-day shoppers
the tanner's own stall, unattended for the moment

factors.fact: That man's false witness cost his family the land outright, years ago.
It has been so long that most of the town has forgotten the dispute entirely.
The old man is frail now and couldn't defend himself against so much as a shove.
Striking a frail old man in the square, whatever the old debt, would make him the one the town judges harshly now.
He has a settled trade and a name in this town that the old grudge could still cost him.

could_also.verb: confronts him with words, in private later
tells the story to a younger listener nearby

would_not.why: beating a frail old man now would cost him the standing he's spent years rebuilding

would_not.verb: forgives it outright and greets him
would_not.why: the debt was real and years haven't actually settled it, whatever the town's forgotten

then: He lets the old man pass, but that evening he finally tells his own grown son the full story of the land, so the debt at least isn't forgotten entirely even if it goes unanswered.
why: The years have shifted what answering the old wrong would cost: the old man is too frail to make it a fair reckoning and the town has moved on, so keeping the account alive in the telling costs him nothing while striking now would cost him everything he's built since.
turns_on: whether anyone else remembers what he did

who: a viper coiled in a sunny patch of rocks
place: a dry hillside path in midsummer, midday heat, footsteps approaching
present: a person's boot, coming down within a foot of the coil
loose scree on either side of the path
the shadow of a passing bird overhead

factors.fact: The boot is about to land close enough to be felt as a real strike, not just a passing vibration.
It has just fed and is sluggish, slower to strike or flee than usual.
The scree to either side offers no fast retreat for a heavy-bodied snake right now.
A rattle or hiss has, every time before, been enough to make heavy footsteps stop or swerve.

could_also.verb: strikes at the boot
tries to slide off into the scree

would_not.why: every close call before this one has been settled by the warning alone, at no cost
silence risks the boot landing on it outright, which a warning has always prevented before

then: The boot jerks back the instant the rattle sounds, and the walker gives the rocks a wide berth the rest of the way past.
why: Being sluggish after feeding means neither a strike nor a full retreat is the safe first move, so the warning that has always worked before is worth trying again, saving the strike itself for if the boot doesn't stop.
turns_on: how close the boot lands to the coil

who: a shepherd tending a flock on common pasture
place: a hillside pasture at midday, a low stone wall marking the customary grazing line
present: a stranger who has let his own goats stray onto the shepherd's side of the wall
the flock of sheep, unsettled by the goats
the shepherd's dog, alert but not yet moving

factors.fact: The wall has marked whose animals graze where for as long as anyone in the valley remembers.
The stranger laughed it off when told his goats had crossed, instead of moving them.
The goats are already cropping grass the shepherd's flock needs to last the season.
The stranger is a grown man like himself, no bigger or smaller, and alone.
The dog can move goats as easily as sheep if given the command.

does.verb: orders the dog to drive back

could_also.verb: argues loudly over the wall
reports it to the village elder later

would_not.why: a shoving match over grass isn't worth what it would cost him with the elders after
the grass they're eating is his flock's for the season and the wall says so

then: The dog pushes the goats back over the wall within a few minutes; the stranger grumbles but doesn't cross again that day, and the shepherd mentions the laughing-off to the village elder that evening anyway.
why: The wall and the season's grass both argue for acting now rather than losing more to grazing, but the stranger's dismissiveness is answered with the dog and a later word to the elder rather than a fight neither the custom nor the stakes actually calls for.
turns_on: whether the stranger is alone or has friends waiting

who: a plow ox, usually placid, startled at midday
place: a field at the edge of the woods, a sudden noise from the treeline
present: a dog from a neighboring farm, barking and nipping at its heels
the plow, still yoked behind it
open field ahead, a fence at the far end

factors.fact: It's yoked to a heavy plow that slows every step it takes.
The dog is small compared to the ox but fast and persistent at the heels.
It has never once turned to fight anything in its life; every startle has ended in bolting.
The field ahead is open all the way to the fence, plenty of room to bolt even dragging the plow.

could_also.verb: kicks out at
stops dead and lowers its head

would_not.why: nothing in its life has ever taught it to fight rather than run
a nipping dog this persistent won't be waited out by standing still

then: It drags the plow in a ragged furrow most of the way to the fence before the farmhand catches up and calls the dog off.
why: An animal with a lifetime of fleeing rather than fighting keeps doing what has always worked, and the open field gives it somewhere to run even yoked, so bolting costs a ruined furrow rather than a fight it has no instinct for.
turns_on: how much room there is to bolt

who: a longtime smallholder, protective of his boundary
place: the fence line between two farms, the day after a stranger bought the neighboring plot
present: a stranger, the new owner of the neighboring land, moving a fence post a stride into the smallholder's field
an old, weathered post the smallholder's father set decades ago
a spade left leaning against the fence

factors.fact: The old post was set by his father and has marked the line unquestioned for decades.
The stranger has already pulled up the old post and is setting a new one further into the field.
A stride of land doesn't sound like much, but strips like it add up over a farm's whole edge.
The stranger is alone, unarmed, and visibly surprised to be confronted.
He could settle this by fetching the old land records instead of his fists.

could_also.verb: demands he put the old post back first
goes to fetch the land records

would_not.verb: lets the new post stand and says nothing
would_not.why: his father's line moving a stride today becomes a field lost within a few seasons if unanswered

would_not.verb: beats him badly over one post
would_not.why: one shove makes the point; more than that turns a boundary dispute into a crime he'd answer for

then: The shove knocks the stranger back a step; words follow, and by evening both have agreed to walk the old line together with the record book rather than move any more posts alone.
why: His father's post being pulled up outright is a direct act, not just a rumor, which justifies an immediate physical answer, but the shove stops at one because the stranger's confusion and the existence of records make a reasoned settlement possible right after.
turns_on: whose father set that fence post

who: a lone, young wolf pushed out of its birth pack, ranging alone
place: the edge of a village's grazing common at dusk, several loose farm dogs gathering
present: four farm dogs, barking from a loose, uneven distance
a flock of sheep penned safely behind a fence
open ground back toward the forest edge

factors.fact: Four dogs are barking, but only two have actually closed the distance; the other two hang well back.
Any two of them together could hurt it badly if they mean it.
It is faster over open ground than any farm dog gathered here.
The forest edge is close enough to reach well before the boldest dog could catch it.
The sheep are fenced and out of easy reach anyway, so there's nothing here worth a real fight.

could_also.verb: snaps at the boldest dog before running
stands and bluffs briefly

would_not.why: even two together is a real risk of injury for no gain, with the sheep already out of reach

would_not.verb: keeps its distance but stays in the open all night
would_not.why: barking dogs that might commit to a real chase aren't worth waiting out in the open

then: It outruns the two dogs bold enough to give chase and is back in the trees within a minute, the other two never having left the yard at all.
why: With the sheep already fenced off there's nothing here to fight for, and even though only two dogs are truly committed, that's still enough risk that its speed toward the forest is worth more than testing them.
turns_on: how many dogs are actually committed to the chase, versus just barking

who: a young man who has just won a rough wrestling match at a village fair
place: a fairground ring, a crowd still gathered, the loser down on the ground
present: the beaten opponent, down and not getting up quickly
a crowd of fairgoers, some cheering, some already losing interest
the opponent's own father, watching anxiously from the crowd

factors.fact: The match ends the moment one man is down and stays down; nothing more is owed after that by the rules of the fair.
The loser fought hard and clean the whole match, nothing underhand.
He can see the loser's father watching, clearly anxious for his son.
The crowd would cheer just as loud for a harder finishing blow as for a gracious one.
He owes the loser nothing more than the win itself; further harm would be his own choice, not the match's due.

could_also.verb: raises his own arms to the crowd first
says something quiet to him alone

would_not.why: the match ended the moment he was down; anything more is a cruelty he wasn't owed

would_not.verb: ignores him and walks off to the crowd
would_not.why: a clean, hard-fought match earns better than being ignored once it's over

then: He pulls the loser to his feet in front of the crowd, and the father's anxious look eases into a nod as his son walks off under his own power.
why: The match's own rule says the win is already settled the moment the opponent went down, so anything past that is the winner's own character showing, and a clean fight from an honorable opponent argues for grace rather than a showier finish the crowd might have cheered just as loud.
turns_on: whether the loser still has family watching
